newsitem.title: USA: EPA overestimated health benefits of clean air plan.
newsitem.headline: EPA overestimated health benefits of clean air plan.

text.p: The Environmental Protection Agency conceded on Wednesday that it had overestimated by one-third the number of premature deaths it could prevent by raising air quality standards.

In a controversial proposal last November to set stricter limits on smog and soot, which sparked an uproar among industry groups, the agency had said new limits on particles in the air could prevent as many as 20,000 premature deaths.
The agency on Wednesday revised the estimate to 15,000 after an independent consultant pointed out an error in the agency's conclusions from one scientific study.
"EPA is continuing to refine this estimate," EPA assistant administrator Mary Nichols said in a statement.

Industry groups and state and local governments, who are worried that new emissions limits will be extremely costly to meet and have questioned the science the EPA used to justify its proposal, were quick to pounce on the agency's error.

"This thing has been based on incomplete science from day one," said Richard Seibert, vice president of the National Association of Manufacturers. "This just shows the problems of the science EPA is using to build the whole rule."
Seibert said EPA should do more research and postpone issuing a final rule, which is due in July.
But EPA officials said the new finding was a natural part of the public comment process and would not slow the agency down in issuing a final rule.
"Clearly, this process is working and is vital to ensuring that the final air quality standards are based on the best available science and protect the public health," Nichols said.
"This particular study was one of 86 different studies that we have considered with regard to the health effects from particulate matter," said another EPA official.
"Fifteen thousand premature deaths is still an important and compelling piece of evidence with regard to why we need to seriously consider changing the standard," he said.
An official representing a coalition of more than 600 big and small companies fighting the proposal questioned whether the revision was even accurate.
"All these calculations of deaths are based on studies based on data that we have not seen yet," said Paul Bailey, speaking for the Air Quality Standards Coalition.
The American Lung Association, which has led the battle for tighter soot restrictions, said the change should not affect EPA's proposal.
"From our perspective it's still too many people dying," said Paul Billings, assistant deputy director of the association. "These are all preventable losses of life."
